existing.title: filter keys must be bare identifiers
existing.summary: filterPredicates now rejects any filter key that is not a bare identifier, although quoteLiteral would keep keys safe and indexable.
existing.failure_scenario: WithFilters(map[string]any{"doc-id":"42"}) returns ErrInvalidFilterKey; the base returned the matching rows.

repro.evidence: HEAD filterPredicates (pgvector.go:487-503) returns ErrInvalidFilterKey for any key that does not match metadataKeyPattern ^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]{0,62}$ (metadata_index.go:21). Both SimilaritySearch (pgvector.go:319) and Search (pgvector.go:394) return that error. Probe probes/v3pgvec/TestProbeFilterKeys at HEAD: doc_id -> '(data.cmetadata ->> 'doc_id') = $4'; 'doc-id', 'file.name', 'x-tenant-id', 'ключ' -> 'filter key must be a bare identifier'. At BASE (pgvector.go:301-302, 366-367) the key was interpolated as '(data.cmetadata ->> 'doc-id') = '42'', a valid jsonb lookup, so those filters returned matching rows. The rejection is intentional (commit ec0ee19; filter_test.go asserts 'a-b', 'a.b', 'ключ' are rejected), but it is still a behaviour break for callers. The base interpolation was also an injection hole, so the fix has to keep the key safe. Rendering the key as a quoted literal (double any ', reject NUL and backslash, as quoteLiteral already does) keeps the expression text 'cmetadata ->> '<key>'' identical to what an index is built on, so indexability does not require the identifier-only gate. The 63-character limit also does not apply to jsonb keys.
repro.comment: Regression: `filterPredicates` now fails with `ErrInvalidFilterKey` on any metadata key that is not a bare SQL identifier, and both `SimilaritySearch` and `Search` return that error. So `WithFilters(map[string]any{"doc-id": "42"})` fails, and so do keys like `file.name`, `x-tenant-id`, non-ASCII keys and keys over 63 characters. The previous release returned the matching rows for all of them. I checked this with a probe calling `filterPredicates` at 355dc71: `doc_id` renders `(data.cmetadata ->> 'doc_id') = $4`, and the other keys all return `filter key must be a bare identifier`. Closing the injection is right, but a jsonb key does not need to be an identifier. If the key is rendered with `quoteLiteral` (double quotes, reject NUL and backslash), the statement keeps the same `cmetadata ->> '<key>'` expression the metadata index is built over, and existing callers keep working. Only `MetadataIndex` names need the identifier gate.

refute.reason: The rejection is deliberate. Commit 504595c added it, and TestFilterPredicatesRejectAKeyThatIsNotAnIdentifier ("a-b", "a.b", "a b") plus narrowing_test.go:170 test for it. Its stated reason does not hold, though. The key is inlined only so the predicate matches the index expression `cmetadata ->> 'key'`. Emitting the key through the existing quoteLiteral would give the same inlined, index-matchable, injection-safe literal. BASE interpolated any key into `(cmetadata ->> '%s')`, so {"doc-id":"42"} matched rows there. HEAD returns ErrInvalidFilterKey even for callers that never declare a metadata index. No changelog or doc mentions this breaking change for callers.

If the key is rendered with `quoteLiteral` (double quotes, reject NUL and backslash), the statement keeps the same `cmetadata ->> '<key>'` expression the metadata index is built over, and existing callers keep working. Only `MetadataIndex` names need the identifier gate.

existing.title: null tool-call arguments rejected
existing.summary: DecodeFields/Decode reject tool-call arguments that are the JSON literal null, which the json.Unmarshal calls it replaced accepted as an empty map.
existing.failure_scenario: The googleai door writes Arguments "null" when Gemini returns a call with nil Args. Replaying that turn makes convertParts fail with ErrNotAnObject, and GenerateContent aborts; Bedrock fails the same way.
existing.evidence: earlier review, vendor behaviour not re-measured

repro.evidence: HEAD toolcall.DecodeFields (arguments.go:30) requires the first token to be '{', so Decode("null") returns ErrNotAnObject. Probe probes/v3nullargs/TestProbeNull: raw="null" gives 'HEAD Decode -> err=toolcall: arguments are not a JSON object: null', while json.Unmarshal (the BASE call) gives map[] err=<nil>. The googleai door marshals part.FunctionCall.Args with json.Marshal (googleai.go:445, 563). genai v1.42.0 declares Args map[string]any `json:"args,omitempty"` and documents it as 'Optional', so a functionCall without args becomes Arguments "null". End-to-end probe TestProbeNullArgsReplay uses a stub HTTP transport whose first response is {"functionCall":{"name":"get_time"}}. HEAD: first turn Arguments="null", then replaying [human, AI tool call, tool response] returns 'toolcall: arguments are not a JSON object: null' before any HTTP request (http_calls=1). BASE: same first turn, replay succeeds (http_calls=2, reply 'noon'). Bedrock (bedrockllm.go:21, 262) uses the same Decode, and its base used json.Unmarshal at bedrockllm.go:235, so a 'null' history (for example one recorded by the googleai door) now fails there too. Ollama cannot produce 'null' itself (ToolCallFunctionArguments marshals nil as {}), but convertToolCall also rejects it now. Still unconfirmed: whether Gemini actually leaves out 'args' for zero-parameter calls. The SDK marks the field optional, no cassette in the repo covers a zero-argument call, and ai.google.dev and cloud docs were blocked by the egress proxy.
repro.comment: Regression: `DecodeFields`/`Decode` reject `"null"` arguments with `ErrNotAnObject`. The `json.Unmarshal` calls they replaced in googleai, Bedrock and Ollama accepted `null` as an empty map. The googleai door itself produces `"null"`: it runs `json.Marshal(part.FunctionCall.Args)`, and genai's `Args` is an optional `omitempty` map. I ran a probe with a stub transport returning `{"functionCall":{"name":"get_time"}}`. At 355dc71 the next `GenerateContent` that replays that turn fails with `toolcall: arguments are not a JSON object: null` before any request is sent; on da7016e the same replay succeeds. Bedrock fails the same way on such a history. How often this happens depends on Gemini leaving out `args` for zero-parameter calls, which the SDK allows but I could not measure live. Suggested fix: treat a literal `null` (and optionally empty input) as `{}` in `DecodeFields`, and/or have the googleai door write `{}` when `Args` is nil.

refute.reason: From the code, DecodeFields("null") gets a nil token from dec.Token(), which is not a Delim, so it returns ErrNotAnObject. BASE googleai (json.Unmarshal into a map) and BASE bedrock (Decoder.Decode into a map) both accepted null as a nil map. HEAD googleai builds Arguments with json.Marshal(part.FunctionCall.Args) at googleai.go:445/563, and a nil map marshals to "null". Replaying that turn goes through toolcall.Decode at googleai.go:703 and fails. Gemini really does omit args for zero-parameter calls (litellm issues #6833/#5055, generative-ai-python #423), so this input occurs in practice. Bedrock's own paths mostly normalise to "{}" (the Converse non-stream path does). Bedrock still fails on any "null" it is handed, for example a Gemini-produced history, where BASE accepted it. No test in HEAD tests for rejecting null on purpose.

existing.title: ANALYZE on every start
existing.summary: ANALYZE on the embeddings table runs on every store start, contrary to the comment saying later starts are only a catalog lookup.
existing.failure_scenario: Every pgvector.New with WithMetadataIndexes samples the whole table while holding the advisory lock, so concurrent store constructions wait on it.

repro.evidence: createMetadataIndexesIfNotExist (metadata_index.go:163-196) runs `ANALYZE <embedding table>` unconditionally, whether or not any CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS created something. The doc comment above the function says 'every start afterwards is a catalog lookup'. Probe probes/v3pgvec/TestProbeAnalyzeEveryStart records statements from two consecutive calls through a fake pgx.Tx. Both starts send [pg_advisory_xact_lock, CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ..., ANALYZE langchain_pg_embedding]. It runs inside init's transaction (pgvector.go:113-148) while holding pg_advisory_xact_lock(pgLockIDEmbeddingTable). That lock id is a single global constant (pgvector.go:24) that createEmbeddingTableIfNotExists also takes (pgvector.go:199), so any store construction in the same database waits for it, including stores on other tables and stores without metadata indexes. The lock is held until commit. One correction to the finding: ANALYZE samples about 300 x default_statistics_target rows, not the whole table. It still also takes a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock, which conflicts with autovacuum and other ANALYZE/VACUUM. This is a performance and startup-latency issue, not a correctness one; the feature is new in this PR.
repro.comment: `createMetadataIndexesIfNotExist` runs `ANALYZE` on the embeddings table on every start, not only after an index was actually built. The function's own comment says later starts are only a catalog lookup. I ran a probe that calls it twice through a recording `pgx.Tx`, and both calls send `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ...` followed by `ANALYZE langchain_pg_embedding`. This happens inside init's transaction while it holds `pg_advisory_xact_lock(pgLockIDEmbeddingTable)`. That lock id is a global constant also taken by `createEmbeddingTableIfNotExists`, so every `pgvector.New` in the database, on any table, waits behind the sampling pass, and it also takes a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock that conflicts with autovacuum. Suggested fix: check `pg_indexes`/`to_regclass` for each derived name first, and run `ANALYZE` only when at least one index was newly created, or leave it to autovacuum.

refute.reason: In createMetadataIndexesIfNotExist, `ANALYZE <table>` runs unconditionally whenever metadata indexes are declared, even when every CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS was a no-op. It runs inside init's transaction while pg_advisory_xact_lock(pgLockIDEmbeddingTable) is held. This contradicts the doc comment that 'every start afterwards is a catalog lookup'. The finding overstates one point: ANALYZE samples about 300×statistics_target rows, not the whole table, so the cost is bounded. It is still a sampled read of a large table on every New, serialised across concurrent constructors. The intent (fresh stats for a new expression index) only needs ANALYZE when an index was actually created. Severity is low (performance), but the code clearly behaves this way. BASE had no metadata indexes.

existing.title: misplaced GetEffort doc comment
existing.summary: GetEffort's doc comment is now attached to HasExplicitTokens because the new methods were inserted between them.
existing.failure_scenario: Godoc shows the GetEffort text as HasExplicitTokens' documentation, and GetEffort has none.

repro.evidence: At HEAD, llms/options.go:119-127 holds the GetEffort doc block, followed with no gap by the HasExplicitTokens comment (128-129) and func (130). DelegatesDepth sits between that and GetEffort at 141. `go doc ./llms ReasoningConfig.HasExplicitTokens` at HEAD prints the whole GetEffort text (DefaultMaxTokens, the effort ladder) and then the HasExplicitTokens sentence. `go doc ./llms ReasoningConfig.GetEffort` at HEAD prints no documentation. At BASE, `go doc` shows the GetEffort doc as expected. This is documentation only and does not change runtime behaviour.
repro.comment: The new `HasExplicitTokens` and `DelegatesDepth` methods were inserted between the `GetEffort` doc comment and `func GetEffort`. As a result `go doc ./llms ReasoningConfig.HasExplicitTokens` prints the whole GetEffort description (DefaultMaxTokens fallback, the low/medium/high ladder), and `go doc ./llms ReasoningConfig.GetEffort` prints nothing. At da7016e GetEffort was documented correctly. To fix, move the `// GetEffort ...` block (lines 119-126) down so it sits directly above `func (r *ReasoningConfig) GetEffort` at line 141.

existing.title: jina comment vs BatchSize
existing.summary: The new comment says _models holds vector dimensions, yet the code still uses those values as the default BatchSize.
existing.failure_scenario: The default batch size is 512, 768 or 1024 depending on the model, derived from dimensions, while the comment claims otherwise; either the comment or the code is wrong.

repro.evidence: At HEAD, embeddings/jina/options.go:67-71 maps the models to 512, 768 and 1024. These are in fact the jina-embeddings-v2 small/base/large vector dimensions. Line 75 (`BatchSize: _models[_defaultModel]`) and lines 86-88 still assign those values to o.BatchSize when the caller did not use WithBatchSize. The new comment at line 86 says "_models holds vector dimensions, not batch sizes" and the very next statement uses them as the batch size. BASE (lines 74, 86-87) had the same defaults, so this is not a behaviour regression: the PR only stopped overwriting a caller-supplied WithBatchSize, and the new unit test checks that part. The harm is a misleading comment and a default batch size that silently depends on the model's dimension. There is no functional failure, because the defaults stay within the Jina request limits.
repro.comment: The new comment says `_models holds vector dimensions, not batch sizes`, but the next line still assigns those values to `o.BatchSize` whenever the caller did not pass `WithBatchSize`, and line 75 does the same. So the default batch size is 512, 768 or 1024 depending on the model's vector dimension, which is what the comment says the numbers are not for. Behaviour is unchanged from da7016e, since only the caller-override fix is new, so this is a clarity issue rather than a regression. Either use a separate default batch-size constant and keep `_models` for dimensions, or reword the comment to say these dimension values are deliberately kept as the legacy default batch size.

refute.reason: The comment and the code do not contradict each other. The comment `// _models holds vector dimensions, not batch sizes.` (options.go:86) is accurate: 512/768/1024 are the jina-embeddings-v2 small/base/large dimensions. Using those numbers as the default BatchSize is unchanged from BASE, which also did `o.BatchSize = _models[o.Model]`. Unit tests pin 512/768/1024 on purpose. Commit fe380f3 ("fix(jina): keep the batch size the caller asked for") only stopped this default from overwriting an explicit WithBatchSize, and a test checks that. The comment points out an old quirk that the PR deliberately kept for compatibility. The defaults stay within Jina's per-request input limits. The comment could say why the values are kept, but that is a wording nit, not a defect.

existing.judge_reason: Not a defect. The comment at embeddings/jina/options.go:86 ("_models holds vector dimensions, not batch sizes") is true: 512/768/1024 are the jina-embeddings-v2 small/base/large dimensions. Using those numbers as the default BatchSize is unchanged from BASE, which also did `o.BatchSize = _models[o.Model]` after the option loop. Commit fe380f3 ("fix(jina): keep the batch size the caller asked for", PAGI-237) changed one thing: the map no longer overwrites an explicit WithBatchSize. The unit tests pin 512/768/1024 as defaults on purpose, and TestTheCallersBatchSizeReachesTheWire covers the fix. So the comment and the code do not contradict each other, as the finding says ("either the comment or the code is wrong"). The comment warns about an old quirk the PR kept for compatibility. At most, the comment could also say why the dimension-derived defaults are kept, which is a wording nit and not worth an inline comment. The earlier thread can be closed as a false positive. Separate observation, not part of this finding and not verified with a probe: at HEAD, WithBatchSize(0) sets batchSizeFromCaller, so BatchSize stays 0. embeddings.BatchTexts then computes len(texts)/batchSize (embedding.go:110), which panics with integer divide by zero. BASE overwrote the 0 with the model's value for known models. If callers pass 0 to mean "default", this is a regression worth checking.
